questions.prompt: In ServiceNow, what is an instance?
options: A complete, independent deployment with its own database, applications, customizations, and users, that does not share data with any other instance
A single application installed on top of a shared, company-wide database with environment flags separating its data
A temporary sandbox that is automatically deleted after 24 hours of use
A licensed add-on product, like Performance Analytics, sold separately from the base platform
A single table within the Now Platform's underlying data model
A snapshot of a form's layout that can be restored later
questions.explain: Lesson 2 defines an instance as a full, independent deployment -- its own database, applications, customizations, and users. Two instances belonging to the same customer never share data; nothing moves between them except through a deliberate mechanism like an Update Set.
questions.distractorExplain: Some SaaS products do let multiple environments share one underlying database with environment flags -- but Lesson 2 is explicit that ServiceNow instances never work that way. Each instance has its own completely separate database with no shared records, which is exactly why an incident created in Development never appears in Production on its own.

questions.prompt: A company's admin team maintains Development, Test/QA, and Production instances. Why can't a configuration change built in Development simply be copied by hand into Production?
options: Because promotion between instances is meant to be deliberate and tracked -- ServiceNow's traditional mechanism, the Update Set, captures changes in one instance so they can be committed into another, rather than silently copied
Because Development and Production instances technically share the same database, so a manual copy would create duplicate sys_ids
Because only a Production instance is allowed to contain Business Rules
Because an Update Set must exist before a Personal Developer Instance can even be requested
questions.explain: Lesson 2 is explicit that promotion between instances is deliberate and tracked, never a silent copy -- Update Sets (and, more recently, Source Control/DevOps integration) exist specifically so changes move between genuinely separate, isolated instances on purpose.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Personal Developer Instance that goes unused for a period of inactivity (commonly around two weeks) goes ________, and must be manually woken up from the developer portal before you can log in again.
questions.explain: Lesson 3 describes hibernation/dormancy as the real limitation of a PDI -- it isn't deleted, just paused, and has to be explicitly woken from developer.servicenow.com before anyone can log back in.

questions.prompt: Match each layer of the Now Platform architecture to what it actually contains.
right: ACLs, Flow Designer workflow, and REST/IntegrationHub integration -- cutting across every other layer at once
Classic UI/UI16 and the newer Next Experience/Workspaces -- a presentation choice over the same underlying data
Tables, fields, and table extension under the Glide Data Model -- purely structural, with no behavior of its own
Forms, lists, and the scripting engine (Business Rules, Client Scripts, Script Includes) that make them behave intelligently
questions.explain: Lesson 4's four-layer model: the database layer is purely structural data (Glide Data Model); the application layer adds forms, lists, and scripting logic; the UI layer is the presentation choice (UI16 vs. Next Experience/Workspaces); and platform services like ACLs, Flow Designer, and integration reach into every layer at once rather than sitting in just one.

questions.prompt: An admin wants to inspect the change_request table directly, even though no module in the Application Navigator currently points at it. What should they type into the navigator's filter box, and why does it work?
options: change_request.list -- the direct-navigation shortcut opens any table's list view directly from its real table name, with no saved module required
change_request.do, because .do always opens a list view instead of a blank form
change.search, because only Favorites can open a table without a module pointing at it
They cannot reach the table at all until a module is created for it first
questions.explain: Lesson 5's direct-navigation shortcut works for any table you have access to, including ones with no module pointing at them at all -- typing <table>.list opens that table's list view immediately, which is exactly why this is the tool admins reach for to inspect a table directly.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the tradeoff between UI16 and a purpose-built Workspace.
options: UI16 gives access to any table or module through one consistent navigation pattern, at the cost of navigating between separate list and form views
A Workspace is generally narrower in scope, built around one job, but faster and more focused for that specific job
Most instances fully replace UI16 the moment a Workspace like Agent Workspace is configured
Workspaces are built with UI Builder or shipped out-of-box by ServiceNow, such as Agent Workspace
Agent Workspace is designed to replace System Properties and other administrative configuration screens
questions.explain: Lesson 6 describes a genuine tradeoff, not a replacement: UI16 is general-purpose but requires navigating between list and form views, while a Workspace is narrower but faster for the one job it's built for. Most instances keep both running side by side, and Agent Workspace is not an administration tool.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a new agent's incident timestamps display in the wrong time zone. This is most likely a personal preference, fixed from the user's own ________ menu -- never from the System Properties application.
questions.explain: Lesson 8 draws this exact distinction: personal preferences like time zone live behind the user's own profile picture/user menu, and any logged-in user can change their own regardless of role -- System Properties is the wrong place to look for a personal display setting.

questions.prompt: Put these Navigation Lab steps in the order the lesson actually performs them.
items: Type incident.list into the Application Navigator's filter box and press Enter to open the table's list view directly
Open the condition builder's filter icon and set Assignment group is Network, then click Run
Open the profile picture / user menu in the top-right corner and confirm the personal time zone preference is correct
questions.explain: Lesson 9 runs this exact sequence: jump straight to the table with the direct-navigation shortcut, build the filter in the condition builder, then route the personal time-zone check to the profile menu rather than System Properties.

questions.prompt: A manager builds a report directly against the task table with no further filtering. Why does the result include incidents, problems, and change requests all mixed together instead of returning nothing?
options: Because incident, problem, and change_request all extend task, so every record on each of those tables is simultaneously a row that satisfies a query against task
Because task is a database view that unions the three tables together only at report-run time
Because ServiceNow randomly samples records from related tables whenever a query returns zero rows
Because task and incident are configured to share identical sys_id values by default
questions.explain: Lesson 11 explains that because incident extends task, every incident record is simultaneously a row that satisfies a query against task -- the same is true for problem and change_request, which is why an unfiltered task report mixes all of them together.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about sys_db_object, sys_dictionary, and a table's standard fields.
options: Every table in the instance, including custom tables, has one row in sys_db_object recording its real name and which table it extends
A column's definition lives in sys_dictionary as its own record, not in a fixed schema file only a DBA can edit
sys_id is a 32-character GUID that functions as a record's unique, permanent primary key
sys_updated_on is stamped once at record creation and never changes again
Adding a new field to the Incident table always requires a database migration script and a server restart
questions.explain: Lesson 10 is specific: sys_db_object holds one row per table, sys_dictionary holds one row per field, and sys_id is the permanent GUID primary key. sys_updated_on refreshes on every save (sys_created_on is the one stamped once), and schema changes happen live through the UI with no migration script or restart.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a field like incident's caller_id, which stores another record's sys_id rather than storing plain text, is called a ________ field.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 defines a reference field as ServiceNow's version of a foreign key -- it stores the sys_id of the record it points to, and the displayed name is a live lookup, not stored text.

questions.prompt: Match each table name to what it actually is in the task hierarchy.
right: Extends sc_request (itself extending task) -- one record per individual requested line item within a catalog order
Extends task directly -- tracks unplanned service interruptions
Extends task directly -- tracks root-cause investigations
Extends task directly -- tracks planned, controlled changes
questions.explain: Lesson 12's task hierarchy: incident, problem, and change_request each extend task directly, while sc_req_item extends sc_request, which itself extends task -- a two-level structure under the Service Catalog's request.

questions.prompt: In ServiceNow, what is a Journal field, such as Incident's Work notes or Additional comments?
options: An append-only field type where every entry a user adds is preserved as its own timestamped, attributed record, instead of overwriting the previous value
A multi-line String field that simply allows more characters than a normal single-line text box
A read-only field that can never be edited by any user, including administrators
A field that automatically deletes its previous value every time a new comment is added
A Reference field that points to a separate log table of system events
A field type only available on custom tables, never on out-of-box tables like Incident
questions.explain: Lesson 16 describes Journal as distinctly ServiceNow: append-only, with every entry preserved as its own timestamped, attributed record -- that's exactly why the Activity formatter shows a running history of every comment ever added, rather than just the latest one.
questions.distractorExplain: A multi-line String field does hold more text per edit, but it still overwrites its entire value on every save -- it has no memory of previous entries. Journal's append-only, timestamped history is a fundamentally different behavior, and it's what specifically powers the Activity formatter's running log, which a plain multi-line String field could never produce.

questions.prompt: A requirement says a new Risk Level field must be one of exactly Low, Medium, High, or Critical, and every record needs a value set before it can save. Which two dictionary-level decisions correctly satisfy this?
options: Set Type to Choice with four sys_choice values, and check the Mandatory flag
Set Type to String, and check the Unique flag
Set Type to Boolean, and check the Read-only flag
Set Type to Reference pointing at sys_user, and leave Mandatory unchecked
questions.explain: Lesson 18's dictionary lab walks this exact reasoning: Choice fits 'a fixed set of options' where String or Boolean don't, and Mandatory is the dictionary flag that enforces the save-time 'cannot be blank' rule stated in the requirement.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about sys_choice and Incident's priority field.
options: A sys_choice row's label (shown in the dropdown) and its value (what's actually stored) are often different
A dependent choice field's options narrow based on what was picked in a controlling field, via a 'Dependent on field' attribute
Incident's priority field is a simple Choice dropdown the agent always picks directly, with no other logic involved
A sys_choice row can be marked inactive to retire an old option without deleting historical records that still reference it
The sequence number on a sys_choice row determines the field's underlying stored value
questions.explain: Lesson 17 is explicit that priority is usually calculated from Impact x Urgency through a lookup matrix, not picked directly -- a bad example of a simple dropdown. Sequence controls display order only, separate from the stored value, and label/value commonly differ.

questions.prompt: Put these three dictionary-lab decisions in the order the lesson makes them, from a one-sentence requirement.
items: Set the new field's Type to Choice, since the requirement calls for a fixed set of options rather than free text
Add four sys_choice rows (Low, Medium, High, Critical) with sequence numbers controlling their dropdown order
Check the Mandatory flag on the dictionary entry so no record can save without a Risk Level set
questions.explain: Lesson 18 runs through type, then values, then constraints -- deciding the field's Type before defining sys_choice rows, and only then enforcing the save-time rule with Mandatory.

questions.prompt: An admin removes the Category field from the Incident form using Form Layout. What happens to existing incident records' Category data?
options: Nothing -- the field's data and its sys_dictionary definition are untouched; Form Layout only controls whether this particular form displays that field
Every existing incident's Category value is permanently deleted from the database
The field is deleted from sys_dictionary, so no other form or report can reference it anymore
The field becomes read-only everywhere else it appears across the instance
questions.explain: Lesson 19 draws a sharp line between hiding a field on a form and deleting it: Form Layout is a view-level decision, never a schema change. The field's definition stays in sys_dictionary, and the data is still there for every other form, report, or list built against the same table.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in a ServiceNow encoded query, such as active=true^priority=1, the character that means AND between two conditions is the ________ character.
questions.explain: Lesson 21 explains that every breadcrumb filter is translated underneath into an encoded query, where ^ means AND and ^OR means OR -- the same sysparm_query syntax used in a bookmarked list's URL.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to what it actually does.
right: A picker that controls which related lists appear on a form, and in what order
A pill shown above a list's columns, displaying one active filter condition in plain English
A right-click column-header action that clusters rows sharing a value without changing which records are in the list
The Configure option that controls which columns a list shows, and in what left-to-right order
questions.explain: List Layout chooses columns (Lesson 20); Group By clusters already-filtered rows without changing the result set (Lesson 20); a breadcrumb shows one active filter condition in plain English (Lesson 21); Configure > Related Lists controls which related lists show on a form (Lesson 22).

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about related lists on a form.
options: A related list on an Incident form, like Related Problems, shows records that are actually stored on the Problem table, not on Incident
An Incident with no linked Problem record shows an empty Related Problems list, not a missing one -- the related list is still configured to appear
A related list is the same relationship as a reference field, read in the reverse direction
Related lists store their own separate copy of the data, independent of the table that actually owns the records
Which related lists appear on a form, and in what order, cannot be changed once a table is created
questions.explain: Lesson 22 is explicit that a related list is a live query against another table's data, run in the reverse direction of a reference field -- the Problem table still owns those records, and the lab in Lesson 23 confirms a configured-but-empty related list still appears rather than disappearing. Configure > Related Lists lets an admin add, remove, or reorder which ones show.

questions.prompt: Why does ServiceNow never let external import data write directly into a live target table like sys_user?
options: Because one malformed row in the source file would either corrupt the live table or crash the load partway through -- staging isolates raw data so bad rows can be fixed and the transform rerun without re-uploading anything
Because sys_user is the only table ServiceNow protects with staging
Because Import Sets are a legal requirement for any table holding personal data
Because a direct write would exceed ServiceNow's row-count licensing limit
questions.explain: Lesson 24 explains the two-stage pattern exists specifically because a direct-write approach either corrupts a live table or crashes partway through on bad data -- staging isolates raw rows so an admin can fix the source data or mapping and rerun the transform.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Transform Map setting that checks whether a matching record already exists in the target table -- updating it if found, inserting a new record if not -- is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 26 defines coalesce as ServiceNow's upsert mechanism -- the field (or fields) used to decide whether a staged row updates an existing record or inserts a brand-new one.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the HR import lab in the order they actually happen.
items: Create a Data Source of Type File and point it at the new_hires CSV
Run the import so rows land unmodified in the auto-created imp_new_hires staging table
Build a Transform Map with imp_new_hires as the source table and sys_user as the target, mapping work_email to email and dept_name to department
Set the coalesce field to email so a returning employee's record updates instead of duplicating
Set up a Scheduled Import so next month's file loads automatically without a manual run
questions.explain: Lesson 27 walks this exact order: configure the Data Source, load into staging, build the Transform Map's field mapping, set coalesce, and only then automate future runs with a Scheduled Import.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ServiceNow Data Source types.
options: JDBC lets ServiceNow query another system's relational database directly, without anyone manually exporting a file first
File is the right Data Source type for CSV, Excel, XML, or JSON files uploaded or attached directly
A Scheduled Import is required before any Data Source can be loaded even once
FTP/SFTP points at a file sitting on a remote server rather than one uploaded by hand
REST / Import Set REST API is the typical pattern for a one-time manual file upload rather than a system-to-system integration
questions.explain: Lesson 25 covers File, JDBC, FTP/SFTP, Web Service, and REST as genuinely different source types. A manual 'Load All Records' run works without any Scheduled Import, and REST is specifically the pattern for system-to-system integration, not one-time manual uploads.

questions.prompt: Why can't a standard ServiceNow Report, no matter how well it's filtered or grouped, show 'open incidents this week versus last week'?
options: A Report runs a live query against the table's current state and has no stored history -- by the time you ran it again later, the earlier count would already be gone; only Performance Analytics's scheduled snapshots retain that history
Because Report Designer does not support the incident table
Because a Report can only ever show one chart type per table
Because comparing two time periods always requires a custom script, in both Reports and Performance Analytics
questions.explain: Lesson 29 draws the entire distinction this way: a Report answers 'what does this look like right now,' with no memory, while PA's collector jobs capture and keep daily snapshots -- which is the only reason a week-over-week trend is answerable at all.

questions.prompt: Match each report/chart type to its best-fit use case.
right: Cross-tabulates two fields at once, e.g. priority down the rows and assignment group across the columns, with a count in each cell
Best for comparing categories side by side, like incidents by assignment group
Buckets records into real calendar intervals (day, week, month) using a date/time field, to show a trend
Best for 'what's the breakdown of a whole,' like open incidents by priority, as slices sized by count
questions.explain: Lesson 28 matches each chart type to the question it answers: Pie for a share of a whole, Bar for comparing categories, Time Series for a trend across calendar intervals, and Pivot Table for cross-tabulating two fields at once.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Performance Analytics ________ job runs on a schedule, typically once a day, and captures a single KPI value as a permanent snapshot.
questions.explain: Lesson 29 names the collector job as the mechanism that makes trend possible -- it runs on a recurrence, typically daily, and captures a snapshot that a live Report structurally cannot reproduce after the fact.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about building a dashboard.
options: A dashboard is a container that arranges existing reports and PA widgets on tabs -- it doesn't generate any new data itself
Reports and PA widgets must already exist as standalone items before they can be added to a dashboard's canvas
Role-based visibility is a minor setting that can safely be added after the dashboard has already been shared with everyone
A dashboard's refresh interval controls how often it automatically re-pulls data for its widgets
Building a dashboard automatically creates the underlying reports it will display
questions.explain: Lesson 30 is explicit that a dashboard is purely a canvas for content that already exists -- reports and widgets have to be built first -- and treats role-based visibility as a core design decision made at build time, not a minor afterthought.

questions.prompt: During the Meridian Freight capstone, why does Lesson 33 insist on actually opening System Definition > Tables and checking incident's 'Extends table' field, rather than simply assuming it extends task because that's the standard pattern?
options: Because a real, unfamiliar instance should be verified rather than assumed -- confirming the hierarchy directly is what turns 'probably true' into documented fact a new admin can stand behind
Because ServiceNow instances randomly change which table incident extends between releases
Because the Extends table field is only visible to users holding the admin role, and never appears on a Personal Developer Instance
Because incident does not actually extend task on most real customer instances
questions.explain: Lesson 33 frames this as the whole point of the capstone: on a real instance with no onboarding document, you confirm the task hierarchy by actually checking the Extends table field, rather than assuming the standard pattern holds -- that's the first line of real documentation, not a guess.

questions.prompt: Put these capstone-kickoff reconnaissance steps in the order Lesson 32 performs them on an unfamiliar instance.
items: Type 'tables' into the Application Navigator's filter box to surface System Definition > Tables
Confirm the base tables task, cmdb_ci, and sys_user actually exist on this instance
Check System Applications > All Available Applications > Installed to confirm Incident, Problem, Change, and Request are actually turned on
questions.explain: Lesson 32 runs this exact reconnaissance order: find the table list first, confirm the expected base tables exist, and only then verify which applications are actually installed and in active use -- rather than assuming any of it.
